name: How to create a unique P
summary:
The hard part is coming up with a unique POV. But here are 3 ways to get started:
1. Change the subject of the category.The key here is to get hyper-specific about what it is you’re actually writing about.
Is it “business news” in general?
Or is it news updates on small businesses?
Or news updates on small businesses in remote locations?
The more specific you can get about the subject you are writing about, the easier it is for readers to decide (in a very binary way) whether this is exactly for them, or exactly not for them.
2. Change the outcome of the category.By changing the outcome you are helping the reader achieve, you are likely moving out of one category of subject matter and into another.
For example, notice the difference between an investing newsletter that promises readers stock recommendations that will make them a lot of money (outcome #1) versus an investing newsletter that promises to teach readers how to navigate emerging cryptocurrency laws (outcome #2).
If everyone else is focused on creating content around “investing best practices,” how can you write about (and solve) a different and even more specific problem?
3. Change the audience of the category.Finally, you can niche down even further by changing who the content is for.
Notice the differences:
Investing 101 For Teenagers
Investing 101 For College Students
Investing 101 For First-Time Parents
Investing 101 For Late Bloomers & Boomers
Just by changing the intended audience, you can radically change which category you are in (and also, by definition, changes the Subject and the Outcomes you write about).

name: 16 lessons for CMOs from Dave Gerhardt
summary:
16 Lessons I Wish I Knew As First Time B2B Marketing Leader
1. Forget the acronyms & best practices, use your brain. Ultimately there are only three ways to grow a business: get more new customers, increase the transaction value, increase how often people buy from you. You can get lost in the MQL PQL SQL SAL definitions and best practices. Get back to the basics and operate from first principles.
2. You need a story to be successful in B2B. Call it a category, call it a movement. Regardless, you need a story that people can bring to their boss about why they should buy your product beyond features + benefits. HubSpot created inbound marketing. Gainsight championed customer success. Drift conversational marketing. Each led through education + expertise and showed people a new way of doing things. Sell the vision and the story.
3. You need to sweat the "offer" - request a demo and contact sales are only going to convert for the highest intent prospects. You need other offers. HubSpot's website grader. Drift did a "test drive" to test the chatbot on your website before talking to anyone. Demandwell has a free SEO audit. Clari has a revenue leakage calculator. These are all smart ideas that are still further down the funnel than ebook but work to get qualified buyers in to eventually talk to sales.
4. Avoid incremental thinking. You can waste so many cycles thinking that the next homepage variation or the email series is going to be the thing that gets you out of the revenue hole. Rarely does "nurturing" solve the problem. Take bigger swings.
5. You must find a way to get on the same page as sales, no matter what. Find a way to put all the internal politics aside. You will never be successful unless you can marketing sales + marketing = revenue *together*. Find out how the VP of sales is comped and do everything in your power to get on the same page. Health teams gives bonuses based on company goals not team goals. Find out and fix it. Manage up to the CEO if needed. Life is 100% easier when sales + marketing have shared revenue goals.
6. Make finance and ops your best friends. YOU HAVE PLENTY TO DO ON YOUR OWN, YOUR JOB IS NOT FINANCE AND OPS I PROMISE YOU!!!! But instead find a way to make them your key business partners. Same way you need to be on the same team as sales, you need to be on the same team with finance and ops. Make them your best friends - collaborate on marketing as a business function Don’t be like 28 year old Dave “I got this myself” - DON’T GET DEFENSIVE - take the help, work together.
7. Show your work and master internal communication. Top complaint: I never know what marketing is doing. If you can’t get the people inside fired up, how will customers be? Top complaint: Marketing is doing a lot, but no idea how it fits our goals. You must always be sharing the bigger picture, related to company goals. Some systems I like: Slack: sharing screenshots, work in progress, teasers, etc. Weekly, monthly, quarterly recaps - here’s what marketing is up to . Take any opportunity to present to the company you can get. Create cross-functional check-ins with marketing, product, sales, CS, finance, ops, together. Marketing is the leadership department as Christopher Lochhead says. Make it that way. Lead by example. You're supposed to be the best communicators in the company right?
8. You must be able to articulate what your marketing strategy is. Don’t get lost in the tactics - see too much of this today. It’s the job of the marketing leader to have a vision for HOW the company does marketing. ABM? Product led? Both? SMB? Mid Market? Enterprise? Be intentional about your approach. You cant take the peanut butter approach and spread average stuff everywhere and expect to win. FOCUS. But also what type of marketing, what brand do you want to be? Have a view on the market, have a view on how you’ll do marketing this year, have a POV on what good marketing looks like. Ex: at Privy we sold to small businesses so we knew they weren't marketing experts and our marketing had to speak to them and they didn't have a lot of time to figure it out, so we had to lead with simple + clear + educational content.
9. You must be able to think short term and long term. Hitting today's goal is great, but what about when the plan jumps 50% next year? You need to be able to build the foundation for that now or you'll wish you did a year from now. Spend 70% of your time on today and 30% of your time on next year/tomorrow. Be disciplined about laying the groundwork for next year and beyond and it will payoff. What will your next channels be? Where can you get future growth from? Start testing and learning now before you need it. Then you can be ready to turn it on.
10. Manage up to the CEO. She cares about two things: revenue and the story. Keep your communication + collaboration tight to those things. She doesnt need to know every detail about what's going on inside of your org and you shouldn't let her. Manage up and get help around revenue and the story. Focus your efforts there.
11. You have to making hiring your job not your side project. People are everything. You know that. Every HBR article ever has said it. But candidates are not going to magically fall on your lap you must treat this like your own marketing program. It's not HR / recruiters job it's your job - no one will know who to hire better than you. Build a brand for yourself in the market. Get religious about sourcing via LinkedIn. Make it your full-time job. Even if you're not hiring you should always be meeting great marketers -- at least so you can model / know what great looks like. Keep a list of your dream team. Make a spreadsheet of names of great people you'd hire if you could one day. You never know.
12. Create your own momentum. It's 2022. You dont need to wait for Gartner or Forrester to write about you. You dont need the product team to ship the one key feature. Marketing is ultimately about content. You can create your own momentum by thinking like a publishing company. Create regular marketing launches. We called them "marketable moments" this can be content, research, reports, events. And then hopefully yes you have product shipping regularly and can do regular product launches too. But stick to a monthly launch calendar. Make some noise every month on your own, no matter what ingredients you have from the company or product team. Set the dates in advance. Dates and deadlines drive action. At Drift we launched the first Tuesday of every month, regardless. It helped us create our own momentum and was a competitive advantage -- PLUS it was contagious and pushed the rest of the the company to ship more too, especially the product team. They wanted to keep up with us.
13. Your job is to get the job done. Doesn't matter if your hire internally, agency, outsource, use an intern or your grandmother. As the marketing leader they are paying you to deliver the result. Put that above everything else especially your ego. That's the biggest difference between the marketing leader and the individual contributor. It's not necessarily your job to do it but its your job to get it DONE.
14. Do the job internally first before hiring externally. Always test and prove - at least get some signal internally. “What should the role of events manager do?” - no idea, you find out. Ex: you think you want to hire a partner marketing person; great make it part of product marketing's role for a quarter to test and learn. Ex: you want to hire for PR. Great. Make it part of your job for a quarter. You’ll never know what good looks like, how to measure, etc. unless you test it first. You can do this for almost any role / any “job" - I've made many mistakes because I didnt do this first.
15. Get comfortable making bets without perfect data. You will rarely have all of the data / perfect data. Ultimately marketing is about making bets. Attribution doesn’t tell you what to do, it’s an input, something to help guide you. Even in our “data driven world”, must be able to act + make a bet + make a gut decision. That’s the skill (and the fun) of this job 
16. Spend the budget. Dont be afraid of it. Use it. That's what it's there for.

name: Masterclass using the community to drive content creation
summary:
• The quality of our content depends on our questions and the people we send those questions to. So, the Databox content team developed a strategy that includes collaboration with subject matter experts. Instead of creating content independently, they send surveys to professionals and create articles based on their answers. ''We're making sure that we're asking the right people. In the early days, it was customers, and then, people who would make good customers. So it's like ABMish, except that we're not pitching the product or anything. [...] We wouldn't open it up to anybody in the market because we would get different answers. So we were very specific about who we want to answer these and which questions we're asking them.''
• Respondents are our content distribution allies. As John explains, the program they developed, where they get answers from experts, allows them to grow their business network. In addition, these partnerships enable Databox to reach new prospects, as the respondents gladly share the articles they are featured in. ''When these people participate in your content, they're gonna share it. So you have a built-in distribution where if I quote 15 people in an article, those 15 people are gonna tweet about it or post it on their LinkedIn. [...] And that list begins to grow. Ten people become 25, and 25 become 75. A year later, you might have a thousand people on that list who have contributed to your content. So, scaling at that point becomes a lot easier. You have all these people to get quotes from. And the more you have, the quicker you're able to wrap new post ideas and get them written. So, while it takes time, you can certainly scale it.''
• Consistency is vital. No one can deny that quality goes before quantity, but in the modern-day business world, you must be visible to your customers. Otherwise, you risk being forgotten as new possibilities pop up by second. John adds, ''We had to be unique. And then, at one point, it was like, 'All right, we have to publish a lot too; frequency helps.' If you're publishing the right stuff and it's good, it helps. When people say publishing frequency doesn't matter, it depends on what your goals are. But if you're starting and trying to gain traction, it matters.''

name: Measuring Engagement Rate in Google Analytics 4
summary:
This episode explores the transition from bounce rate to engagement rate in Google Analytics 4 (GA4) as a more accurate measure of visitor interaction on websites. It discusses how engagement rate provides a better understanding of user behavior by considering time spent on the site, page views, and goal completions, offering insights into improving website performance.

KEY THEMES
• Transition from Bounce Rate to Engagement Rate — GA4 introduces engagement rate as a more meaningful metric than bounce rate.
• Understanding Engagement Rate — Engagement rate is calculated based on user interactions like page views, time spent, and goal completions.
• Improving Engagement Rate — Strategies to enhance website engagement through content and design optimization.

MAIN INSIGHTS
• Insight 1: Engagement rate in GA4 is calculated by dividing engaged sessions by total sessions.
• Insight 2: An engaged session is defined as a visit where a user views more than one page, spends over 10 seconds on the site, or completes a goal.
• Insight 3: The average engagement rate across 65 client websites is 55%, with organic traffic sources generally showing higher engagement.
• Insight 4: Bounce rate in GA4 is now the inverse of engagement rate, focusing on sessions without significant interaction.
• Insight 5: Customizing reports in GA4 can help highlight engagement metrics, aiding in better analysis and decision-making.

FRAMEWORKS & CONCEPTS
• Engagement Rate — A metric in GA4 that measures the percentage of sessions with active user interaction.
• Adjusted Bounce Rate — A concept where bounce rate is adjusted to account for time spent on a page, similar to engagement rate.

NOTABLE QUOTES
"Jeff Sauer: 'The idea of engagement rate in GA4 is almost too good to be true. Gone are the days of relying on bounce rate.'"
"Analytics experts have been using engagement rate for years, but they’ve called it something else."

ACTION ITEMS
→ Customize GA4 reports to make engagement rates more visible and actionable.
→ Implement strategies to increase engagement rates, such as adding internal links, videos, and detailed content to web pages.

name: Improving email open rates
summary:
This episode focuses on strategies to improve email open rates, emphasizing the importance of sender name, subject line, and preheader text. It highlights insights from top marketers and provides actionable tips to optimize email marketing efforts, making it a valuable resource for anyone looking to enhance their email campaigns.

KEY THEMES
• Email Marketing Optimization — Techniques to increase email open rates by focusing on sender name, subject line, and preheader text.
• Personalization in Email — The impact of using personal names over company names to increase email engagement.
• Data-Driven Strategies — The use of analytics and testing to refine email marketing tactics for better results.

MAIN INSIGHTS
• Insight 1: Using a personal name in the sender field can significantly increase email open rates.
• Insight 2: Sentence case subject lines are more effective as they mimic personal communication.
• Insight 3: Short subject lines, ideally around seven words, perform better, especially on mobile devices.
• Insight 4: Including numbers in subject lines can increase their visual prominence and make emails more appealing.
• Insight 5: Re-sending emails to non-openers can boost open rates by 15% to 30%.

FRAMEWORKS & CONCEPTS
• The Three P's of Email Signup Boxes — A concept for creating high-converting email signup forms.
• Email Authentication (DKIM, DMARC, SPF) — Technical standards to improve email deliverability by verifying sender identity.

NOTABLE QUOTES
"Ann Handley: 'Your From line matters more than your Subject line.'"
"Joanna Wiebe: 'Be really conscious of your From name as, on mobile, it’s got way more visual prominence than your subject line does.'"

ACTION ITEMS
→ Optimize the sender name to be more personal and relatable to increase open rates.
→ Use sentence case for subject lines to enhance readability and mimic personal communication.
→ Test different subject lines on social media to determine which are most engaging before using them in emails.

name: Category Design Fundamentals
summary:
This episode delves into the fundamentals of Category Design, emphasizing the importance of creating a distinct category for business success. It introduces frameworks and insights for identifying and developing unique business categories, which are crucial for standing out in competitive markets.

KEY THEMES
• Category Design — The necessity of creating a unique business category to avoid failure.
• Frameworks for Differentiation — Tools and frameworks to help businesses identify and establish their unique category.
• Brand vs. Category — The pitfalls of focusing on brand over category.

MAIN INSIGHTS
• Insight 1: Category Design is crucial for a company's success, even more so than having a legendary product or team.
• Insight 2: The Category Design Scorecard provides a framework to evaluate whether a company is a true category creator.
• Insight 3: The Big Brand Lie highlights the mistake of prioritizing brand over category creation.
• Insight 4: Extending brands across multiple categories can dilute their impact, as seen with examples like Google+.
• Insight 5: The 8 Category Levers offer strategies to differentiate a business by altering various aspects like brand, experience, and pricing.

FRAMEWORKS & CONCEPTS
• The Magic Triangle — Highlights the importance of having a legendary category in addition to a product and company.
• The Category Design Scorecard — A tool for spotting true category creators based on specific criteria.

NOTABLE QUOTES
"Category Design is the single point of failure for companies."
"The single biggest mistake companies make is marketing their brand—and not their category."

ACTION ITEMS
→ Evaluate your business using the Category Design Scorecard to identify if you are a true category creator.
→ Utilize the 8 Category Levers to differentiate your business in the market.

name: Setting a top referral program
summary:
This episode delves into the mechanics and strategic value of referral programs, using Dropbox's innovative approach as a case study. It highlights the advantages of referral programs over traditional marketing channels, their historical roots, and the nuances of designing effective referral strategies. The discussion also covers the limitations and evolution of referral programs as products mature.

KEY THEMES
• The strategic advantage of referral programs over traditional marketing channels.
• The historical evolution and implementation of referral programs.
• Design considerations and best practices for effective referral programs.

MAIN INSIGHTS
• Insight 1: Referral programs can significantly reduce customer acquisition costs by leveraging existing users to attract new ones.
• Insight 2: Dropbox's referral program, offering storage space as an incentive, was a pivotal moment in the adoption of referral strategies by startups.
• Insight 3: Referral programs are particularly effective for products with high acquisition costs and natural word-of-mouth potential.
• Insight 4: The effectiveness of referral programs diminishes over time as the product's natural virality takes precedence.
• Insight 5: Designing a referral program requires careful consideration of the incentive structure, targeting new users, and aligning with user behavior.

FRAMEWORKS & CONCEPTS
• Network Effects — Utilizing a product's user base to drive growth through referrals.
• The Cold Start Problem — A concept describing the challenges of starting and growing new startups via network effects.

NOTABLE QUOTES
"A successful referral program can be 20-30% of your acquisition mix, as one of several acquisition loops."
"The real question is, WHERE do you make the ask? And my answer is simple: Ask many times, in many places, with different messages."

ACTION ITEMS
→ Integrate referral asks into main user flows and key transaction points to maximize engagement.
→ Consider 'holidizing' referral campaigns to align with major events and increase user participation.

name: Lessons from Andrew Wilkinson
summary:
This episode features Andrew Wilkinson, co-founder of Tiny Capital, discussing his experiences in acquiring 40 companies, the challenges of competing with venture-backed firms, and personal insights on happiness and learning from mistakes. It provides valuable lessons for entrepreneurs and business leaders on navigating the complexities of business acquisitions and personal growth.

KEY THEMES
• Business Acquisitions — Insights from acquiring 40 companies and the lessons learned.
• Competing Independently — Strategies for competing with venture-backed companies.
• Personal Growth — The pursuit of happiness and learning from mistakes in business.

MAIN INSIGHTS
• Insight 1: Acquiring 40 companies has provided a wealth of experience and lessons in business management.
• Insight 2: Competing as an independent company against venture-backed firms requires unique strategies and resilience.
• Insight 3: Mimetic desire can influence personal and business decisions, often leading to unnecessary competition.
• Insight 4: Recovering from million-dollar mistakes is part of the learning process in business.
• Insight 5: Finding happiness in business requires looking beyond financial success.

FRAMEWORKS & CONCEPTS
• Mimetic Desire — The concept that people desire things because others desire them, influencing competition and business decisions.

NOTABLE QUOTES
"Wilkinson: 'Recovering from million-dollar mistakes is part of the learning process.'"
"Wilkinson: 'Finding happiness in business requires looking beyond financial success.'"

→ Develop strategies to compete effectively with venture-backed companies without compromising your values.

name: The three marketing metrics that matter
summary:
This episode of Lochhead on Marketing discusses the three marketing metrics that truly matter: driving revenue, building category potential, and converting this potential into market cap. Christopher Lochhead emphasizes the importance of these metrics in creating sustainable value and growth for a company.

KEY THEMES
• Revenue Generation — Marketing should consistently drive revenue to ensure long-term success.
• Category Potential — Building and revolutionizing market categories is crucial for creating demand and growth.
• Market Cap Conversion — Transforming category potential into market cap through investor perception is essential for enduring business value.

MAIN INSIGHTS
• Insight 1: Marketing activities should lead to consistent revenue generation to be considered effective.
• Insight 2: Brand advertising and awareness campaigns are secondary to having a strong revenue-generating product.
• Insight 3: Building category potential is vital for creating demand and converting it into revenue.
• Insight 4: Investors prioritize potential over performance when evaluating growth companies.
• Insight 5: The perception of future growth is more critical than current revenue for market cap.

FRAMEWORKS & CONCEPTS
• The Magic Triangle — Product, company, and category design that leads to capturing a significant share of the market economics.
• Category Design — Creating or revolutionizing a market category to drive demand and growth.

NOTABLE QUOTES
""If it doesn’t make the cash register sing consistently, it ain’t got that thing.""
""Investors in growth companies and stocks buy potential, not performance.""

ACTION ITEMS
→ Focus marketing efforts on activities that directly drive revenue.
→ Prioritize building category potential to create long-term demand and growth.

name: Copywriting Frameworks
summary:
BAB: before-after-bridge.
• Before: The pain point your audience is facing. Like driving behind a Porsche in a car that’s not a Porsche.
• After: What life is like when that pain is resolved. Hands grip a sport steering wheel. The road ahead is all yours.
• Bridge: The solution—your product. The bridge that takes you from before to after.

That simple statement encapsulates the next framework, PAS: problem-agitate-solve.
• Problem: The pain point. Ferry couldn’t find his dream car.
• Agitate: Agitate the problem. Heighten the negative emotions it provokes—frustration, anger, fear—or the pain it causes. Add some drama.
• Solve: Your product is the solution. Ferry built his dream car: a Porsche.

The third framework is AIDA: attention-interest-desire-action.
• Attention. Grab attention with an eye-catching headline, image, or both.
• Interest. Nurture interest and intrigue. This ad does that by describing the experience of driving a Turbo: “400 horses. Zero to sixty in just over four heartbeats.”
• Desire. Stimulate desire. Want “some very serious amusement”? To get it…
• Action. Take action. Call 1-800-Porsche.

name: Mimetic Desire w/ luke Burgis
summary:
This episode of The Knowledge Project Podcast features entrepreneur and educator Luke Burgis discussing the concept of mimetic desire. Burgis explains how understanding this concept, based on the teachings of René Girard, can help individuals connect the dots between their current state and their aspirations, highlighting the imitative nature of human behavior and the pitfalls of desiring things we don't truly need.

KEY THEMES
• Mimetic Desire — Understanding how our desires are influenced by others and the implications of this on our lives.
• Decision Making — The importance of context and environment in making decisions.
• Influence of Relationships — How the people we choose to surround ourselves with impact our desires and outcomes.

MAIN INSIGHTS
• Insight 1: Mimetic desire explains why people often want things they don't need, as desires are imitative.
• Insight 2: The circumstances or 'soil' in which decisions are made are critical and often overlooked.
• Insight 3: Identifying powerful mediators in our lives can help understand the root causes of problems.
• Insight 4: Intentionally choosing the people we are closest to is crucial for shaping our desires.
• Insight 5: Desires are path dependent, meaning following a particular desire can lead to different outcomes.

FRAMEWORKS & CONCEPTS
• Mimetic Desire — A concept by René Girard explaining that our desires are imitative.
• Layered Thinking — A decision-making framework involving rational, tacit, and potentially other layers.

NOTABLE QUOTES
"I absolutely think that choosing in an intentional way the people that we’re closest to is the most important thing that we can do to affect what we want."
"Desires are path dependent, and one desire can bring us, if we follow that desire, to a place where we’re in a different position than we were when we started."

ACTION ITEMS
→ Identify and understand the mediators in your life to better manage your desires.
→ Be intentional about the people you choose to surround yourself with to influence your desires positively.

name: A Technical SEO masterclass
summary:
Key Insights
• Be patient, and you'll see SEO success. If you have a new site, you will probably have difficulty finding growth opportunities. And SEO, the process of improving the quality and quantity of traffic on your website, will help you grow. According to Steve, one of the issues with SEO is that it's a lot harder to succeed today than it was ten years ago, and you have to be patient before you see the results. "There was a lot of spam that would typically be able to get you to page one or even position one. And now it's a much more complicated game than it once was. Not everybody knows that going in, and there are a lot of people who have failed because of that. And that's where you see a lot of naysayers come into the fore. So there are always gonna be those people who've had tremendous success, those companies that have crushed it with SEO. But then there are gonna be even more of them who have failed and wasted money because it also takes a ton of patience. And if you don't have that patience or the right person guiding your strategy, you're probably going to fail."
• Use "People Also Ask" on Google to find blue ocean opportunities. If you are trying to optimize your content and grow your website but find traffic falling, it’s probably because you are using the wrong strategies. Steve notes that using "People Also Ask" questions on Google is a helpful tactic to find blue ocean opportunities. "Those are accordion menus that appear in the search results when you type in pretty much any query nowadays. So Google is trying to guess the intent or guess the possible other questions that people are asking and trying to make your search experience that much shorter and more efficient. So targeting those questions can be extremely valuable because people don't always know what they're searching for at the beginning, and Google's actively trying to funnel people into the answer that they want."
• SEO Minion is a handy tool for everyday SEO tasks. According to Steve, you can mine "People Also Ask" questions with a tool called SEO Minion, which is also extremely valuable. "If you just go to seominion.com, you can download the Chrome extension and literally expand 200 'People Also Ask' questions and copy them to a spreadsheet in one click. You can get a ton of interesting topics with that. You can then take those URLs that are ranking for those 'People Also Ask' questions and put them into Ahrefs' batch analysis to see which of those questions and pages gets a lot of organic traffic and try to go after those. [...] You can also take those questions and then run them through a keyword clustering tool like keywordcupid.com. It will Google each of those questions, and it will look for similarities in the search results. When it sees similar search results for different keywords, it's going to suggest that you group those keywords together in one piece of content. So it's an efficient way of clustering those types of question-based keywords en masse."
Episode Highlights
Using SEO Minion and Ahrefs to Get Valuable Data
“If for some reason your keywords do not trigger ‘People Also Ask,’ just put ‘What is’ in front of your main keyword, and then you’ll start to get those questions. And basically, you install that SEO Minion plugin. So go to seominion.com and just go to the Chrome store from there and then install that extension. And then, when you’re on the SERP itself, SEO Minion will be overlaid on the right-hand side, and then you would just click ‘Expand.’ So you can expand 5, 10, 20 results up to 200 results. And then, click ‘Go’ […] Once it’s done expanding all that, it’s going to copy it to your clipboard. Then, head over to Excel or Google Sheets and paste those results in. So you’ll be pasting the ‘People Also Ask’ question, the title tag, the URL, and the meta description. So, you have four columns for all of that. And, from there, if you want to see which of those ‘People Also Ask’ topics are getting the most traffic, you can take those URLs and put them into a tool like Ahrefs, which has a thing called batch analysis, where you can just dump up to 200 URLs and get a bunch of valuable data on those URLs.”
How to Use Data from Ahrefs
“There are a couple of things you can do to improve your chances of replicating your topic and being successful with it. The thing that I’ve done in the past, which has worked really well, is to have a note on my email list, SEO Notebook, where I email a piece of strategy every week. And one of the notes was, ‘Put these PAAs into Ahrefs and filter by traffic. And then also sort those rows by their domain rating.’ So, a site with a low domain rating means that it’s a site with not many links, and it’s most likely a newer site. So, if you see a newer site with a bunch of traffic for a keyword that is triggering PAAs and is also ranking, that is a very prime opportunity for you to create a piece of content. Because you see right in front of your eyes that this site, that’s not mature at all, is able to rank with a very thin backlink profile and just on the merits of the content itself. So, you can identify some really easy wins that are going to be closely related.”
Steve’s Case Study with “People Also Ask” at FreshBooks
“Prior to becoming a freelance consultant, I had worked at FreshBooks for about two years. And then, I ended up actually becoming a consultant for FreshBooks after I left the company as an employee in 2020. But when I was there, my boss Chris Cisco came up to me and said, ‘Steve, I need a thousand articles,’ and then he walked away. That’s all he said to me. So I was like, ‘Okay, I have a content background; he knew who he was coming to.’ But, at that time, I also had no idea where to start to produce a thousand articles. That was obviously a huge challenge. And I thought, ‘Hey, what can I do?’ And then, it was like that cliche moment — I was in the shower, and I was like, ‘People Also Ask, we’ve got to do it like that. That’s where we start.’ So we started mining ‘People Also Ask’ questions around accounting, invoicing, entrepreneurship, taxes, and all those things closely related to FreshBooks. And we got thousands of them.”

name: How to create great B2B messaging
summary:
It's a 3-phase (neverending) loop:
--> research--> write--> validateRESEARCH: Things you need to know *before* being able to write messaging that resonates
1. Find out their biggest pains and desired gains, in priority order - this will inform your information hierarchy
2. Identify their jobs to be done via JTBD survey
3. Understand the competitive landscape and positioning of key alternatives (so you can lean into your onlyness)
WRITE: 10 steps to a concise yet compelling pitch
1. Create an outline, structure the different content blocks in the order of their pain and gain priorities
2. If you don't have any copy yet, write the vomit draft first. Just get something on the blank canvas. Then edit.
3. Lead with the category: answer 'what is it?'
4. Present your value proposition: make them want it
5. Communicate your onlyness as soon as you can
6. Write the subheads. Make each one sum up the block that follows. It needs to communicate the main idea without people having to read the paragraph.
7. Write the paragraph copy. Then ask: how can we make it shorter? Cut 30-50%. Short, choppy sentences. More periods, fewer commas. Run paragraphs through the Hemingway app.
8. Edit the whole thing line by line for clarity: how would people say this in an actual conversation? Out with the jargon. Add specificity.
9. Edit each block for relevance and value: is what we're saying aligned with their priorities and challenges at hand? How can we communicate more value?
10. Differentiation check: are we making it clear why choose us? How we're better/different?
VALIDATE: does it resonate?
1. Once your v1 is done, conduct message testing with Wynter. You will find out what's unclear, irrelevant, doesn't communicate enough value, creating confusion and putting them off. Now that you know these things, you can edit, and re-test to see if you eliminated all friction.
2. When in doubt about which headline/value prop to go with, should you say X or Y, run a preference test with Wynter.
 Messaging advice
Speak in full sentences in your subheads

name: Andy Galpin vs Huberman on strength training
summary:
In this episode of the Huberman Lab podcast, Andrew Huberman hosts Dr. Andy Galpin, an expert in exercise science, to discuss comprehensive strategies for building fitness across various levels. They delve into the principles of strength training, hypertrophy, endurance, flexibility, and the importance of proper hydration and nutrition. The conversation emphasizes the significance of understanding exercise mechanisms and tailoring training protocols to individual goals, whether for recreational exercisers or professional athletes.

KEY THEMES
• The Science of Exercise — Understanding the mechanisms behind different types of fitness adaptations.
• Tailored Fitness Protocols — Customizing exercise routines based on individual goals and fitness levels.
• Integration of Strength and Endurance — Exploring the relationship and potential interference between strength and endurance training.

MAIN INSIGHTS
• Insight 1: Exercise choice does not determine adaptation; execution and application of exercises are crucial.
• Insight 2: Strength training requires high intensity and low repetition ranges, focusing on neural adaptations.
• Insight 3: Hypertrophy can be achieved with a wide range of repetitions (5-30) as long as sets are taken to muscular failure.
• Insight 4: Eccentric exercises can help activate difficult-to-target muscles and are beneficial for strength development.
• Insight 5: The interference effect between strength and endurance training is often overstated, especially with moderate endurance activities.

FRAMEWORKS & CONCEPTS
• Henneman's Size Principle — Describes the recruitment of motor units from smallest to largest based on the force required.
• SAID Principle (Specific Adaptation to Imposed Demand) — The body adapts specifically to the demands placed on it.

NOTABLE QUOTES
"Dr. Andy Galpin: 'The concepts are actually fairly few, but the methods are many.'"
"Andrew Huberman: 'Intentionality matters for both strength and hypertrophy training.'"

ACTION ITEMS

KEY THEMES
• Impact of Small Behaviors — Small changes in daily habits can lead to significant health improvements.

MAIN INSIGHTS
• Insight 1: Delaying morning caffeine intake by 90 to 120 minutes after waking can help avoid afternoon energy crashes.
• Insight 2: The molecule adenosine builds up in the brain and body the longer one is awake, influencing energy levels.
• Insight 3: Lack of impulse control is a major cause of disorder and dysfunction in the world.
• Insight 4: Immediate action without overthinking can activate the nervous system into a productive state.
• Insight 5: Adults are less likely to change behavior unless it is through self-directed efforts, unlike children.

FRAMEWORKS & CONCEPTS
• Neural Plasticity — The nervous system's ability to rewire and learn new behaviors and skills.
• Self-Directed Plasticity — The concept that adults can change behaviors effectively through self-directed efforts.

NOTABLE QUOTES
"Most of the disorder and dysfunction in the world is caused by lack of impulse control."
"Forget trying to get people to change, it does not work. It works with children, it does not work with adults unless it’s self-directed plasticity."

ACTION ITEMS

→ Engage in immediate action without overthinking to set your nervous system into a productive mode.

name: Evaluating the fit for TIk Tok Ads
summary:
1. Can you commit the budget to test TikTok ads properly? Every new channel has a cost of entry, and you have to spend to learn. We recommend setting aside 10% - 30% of your ad budget to test this channel properly. It’ll likely take 6-10 weeks to test and validate TikTok as a paid acquisition channel.
2. Does TikTok align with your product? TikTok ads perform well for DTC ecom brands and mobile apps. DTC ecom brands selling visual products with broad appeal, short sales cycles, and AOVs between $25 - $100 tend to get the most out of TikTok. Similarly, mobile apps and games work well since free app installs are low-friction. TikTok ads can work for many other types of products, but consider how your product aligns with the channel before testing.
3. Do you have the capacity to focus on TikTok as a separate channel in your ad mix? TikTok is an entirely different beast than Facebook. To give TikTok ads a fair shot, you'll need to invest resources into producing a high volume of channel-specific creatives that you can test diligently. Whether you make them yourself or partner with content creators, having a high volume of creatives ready to go is essential.
4. Have you seen success with Snapchat ads, IG Reels, or IG Stories? If you've had success with any of these channels and want to diversify, TikTok is a logical next step. TikTok can have cheaper CPAs, cheaper CPMs, and higher quality traffic than Snapchat or Instagram. You can try repurposing Snapchat/IG assets because these types of ads are typically vertical UGC videos, precisely the kind of content that performs best on TikTok. And if you have the original video content, even better. You can cut new ads, making full use of TikTok's audiovisual publishing tools to achieve the right aesthetic.

name: SEO masterclass fo B2B marketers
summary:
This episode is a masterclass on demystifying SEO for B2B marketers, focusing on its importance as a fundamental piece of modern marketing strategy. Mitch, an experienced SEO professional, shares insights on integrating SEO into B2B marketing, the roles involved, and how to measure its success, making it a crucial listen for marketers looking to enhance their organic search strategies.

KEY THEMES
• SEO as a Distribution Channel — SEO should be viewed as a distribution channel similar to email or paid ads, and it should be integrated into the demand generation side of marketing.
• Content and SEO Alignment — The importance of aligning content creation with SEO goals, ensuring that content is optimized for search from the outset.
• Long-term SEO Investment — SEO is a long-term investment that compounds over time, providing sustainable traffic and revenue growth.
• SEO Measurement and Attribution — Challenges and strategies for measuring SEO success, including focusing on revenue attribution and understanding the buyer's journey.
• In-house vs. Agency for SEO — Considerations for managing SEO in-house versus outsourcing, depending on team capabilities and business needs.

MAIN INSIGHTS
• Insight 1: SEO should be managed within the demand generation team as a distribution channel, not just a brand exercise.
• Insight 2: Effective SEO requires a balance between content creation and technical infrastructure, with a focus on producing high-quality, audience-targeted content.
• Insight 3: SEO investment should be justified by its potential to drive long-term, sustainable traffic and lower customer acquisition costs compared to paid channels.
• Insight 4: Measuring SEO success should focus on revenue attribution, meetings, and deal flow, rather than just traffic metrics.
• Insight 5: Content should be created with SEO in mind from the start, using briefs that include target keywords to ensure alignment with search intent.

FRAMEWORKS & CONCEPTS
• ICE Framework — Infrastructure, Content, and Endorsements (links) as the three pillars of a successful SEO strategy.
• Share of Search Report — A tool to compare your search market share against competitors and identify missed opportunities.

NOTABLE QUOTES
""SEO is not a silver bullet, but it's a fundamental piece of a modern B2B marketing strategy.""
""Google is the single largest social experiment that has ever happened from a data perspective.""

ACTION ITEMS
→ Start with low-funnel content to drive immediate revenue opportunities and work upwards to mid and top-funnel content.
→ Ensure SEO and content teams collaborate closely, using content briefs that include SEO keywords to guide writers.

name: The basics Account Based Marketing
summary:
This episode of the Predictable Revenue Podcast focuses on Account-Based Marketing (ABM) and its significance in B2B marketing. Host Sarah Hicks and guest Simeon Atkins discuss the strategic, targeted nature of ABM, its benefits for sales and marketing alignment, and common pitfalls to avoid. They also provide a step-by-step guide to implementing an effective ABM strategy, emphasizing the importance of data and sales intelligence tools.

KEY THEMES
• Account-Based Marketing — A strategic approach targeting specific high-value accounts.
• Sales and Marketing Alignment — Essential collaboration for successful ABM implementation.
• Data-Driven Strategies — Utilizing sales intelligence tools for effective targeting and engagement.

MAIN INSIGHTS
• Insight 1: ABM is a strategic form of B2B marketing that focuses on targeting specific accounts with high ROI potential.
• Insight 2: Successful ABM requires close collaboration between sales and marketing teams to align on targets and messaging.
• Insight 3: An omni-channel approach is crucial in ABM to effectively engage decision-makers through various platforms.
• Insight 4: Common mistakes in ABM include targeting too broad an audience and lack of alignment between sales and marketing.
• Insight 5: Sales intelligence tools like SimilarWeb are vital for identifying target accounts and understanding their needs.

FRAMEWORKS & CONCEPTS
• Account-Based Marketing (ABM) — A targeted approach focusing on specific high-value accounts.
• Omni-Channel Approach — Using multiple channels to engage different decision-makers effectively.

NOTABLE QUOTES
"ABM cannot be successful unless you have sales and marketing working closely together."
"If done well, ABM can help revenues and logos skyrocket."

ACTION ITEMS
→ Assemble an ABM team with both sales and marketing reps who understand customer pain points and solutions.
→ Identify your ideal customer profile and target accounts with high strategic value.
→ Utilize sales intelligence tools to gather data on target accounts and decision-makers.

summary:

The conversation covers the importance of understanding your business model for determining optimal bounce rates, the transition to Google Analytics 4 (GA4), and how to effectively use data to drive business growth.

KEY THEMES
• Understanding Bounce Rates — The importance of knowing what bounce rate means for your specific business model.
• Transition to GA4 — Embracing the new Google Analytics 4 platform and its implications for data analysis.
• Data-Driven Decision Making — Using analytics to inform smart SEO and marketing strategies.

MAIN INSIGHTS
• Insight 1: Bounce rates should be evaluated in the context of your specific business model rather than industry averages.
• Insight 2: Proper implementation and setup of Google Analytics is crucial for meaningful bounce rate data.
• Insight 3: GA4 is the future of analytics, and marketers should familiarize themselves with it despite comfort with universal analytics.

FRAMEWORKS & CONCEPTS
• Bounce Rate — A metric indicating the percentage of visitors who leave a site after viewing only one page.
• GA4 (Google Analytics 4) — The latest version of Google Analytics, offering advanced tracking and analysis capabilities.

NOTABLE QUOTES

name: the origins of Discord
summary: During his early career, Jason Citron stepped away from two stalled businesses and pivoted—twice—to something far more successful. The second time he did it, he created one of the most popular social media platforms in the world. It started at age 13 when Jason had a “holy crap” moment, discovering he could make his own video games. His first video game company morphed into a social platform for gamers, and after he sold it, he couldn't resist launching another. When that business failed to get traction, he again re-imagined it as a digital space for gamers to gather, and in 2015, Discord was born. Today, the platform has 150 million monthly users, and is a gathering place not just for gamers, but for anyone who wants to connect with friends

name: 6 traits to become a B2B marketer
summary:
Use these 6 tips to accelerate your marketing career: 
 
1. Commit
 
Set a goal for where you want to be & make a commitment to getting there. This requires patience & looking at this with a long-term view. 
 
It’s been 7 years since I committed to taking my career & my life to the next level on the plane ride home from a Sales Kickoff meeting in 2016. 
 
2. Get on a team that’s GROWING. It’s crazy how much you grow with it
 
Set yourself up for success by getting on the right team where you can learn, build connections, and have opportunities to get promoted or work on exciting projects. 
Being on the wrong team or in the wrong company can be a giant detractor for your personal & professional growth. If that's you, get on a new team ASAP.
 
3. Start a side project (to learn & build skills)
 
Start a podcast, or a community, or a social media account, or an e-commerce store - there’s a ton of options. This will get you experience in business, marketing, and producing content that people want. 
 
Instead of climbing the corporate ladder for 6 years, working on a side project gives you the opportunity to leapfrog everyone because you’ve taken initiative to build tangible skills on your own time.
 
I started my first side project in 2013 where I built a 6-figure e-commerce business from my bedroom. I had 2 other side projects before starting Refine Labs
 in 2019. These projects built skills that set me up for success in the future.
 
4. Consume information to learn (be very selective about who you get information from)
 
There’s a ton of misinformation out there. Be intentional about who you get your information from. This creates focus & consistency that’s been a game changer for me since 2016. 
 
5. Always think like you’re the CEO
 
This is how you accelerate your specialized & practical business knowledge. In every situation, practice thinking like you’re the CEO. This forces you to elevate from the weeds of your current role & see the whole landscape. It forces you to think strategically. 
 
You can identify the most important areas of the business & then assemble a plan for how you’d solve them. Oftentimes, your projects will be approved & you’ll be chosen to lead it. 
6. Find mentors (oftentimes they find you)
Instead of asking people to be your mentor, try putting yourself in the environments where you get to work with people like that every day. When you put yourself in the right situations with the right people with the right mindset, mentors will oftentimes find you (it doesn’t even feel like mentorship while it’s happening, but only in retrospect).

• Valuation challenges of Liga MX — Despite its popularity, Liga MX clubs have lower valuations compared to MLS teams.
• Strategic investments and growth opportunities — Investments in Liga MX, such as the Necaxa deal, highlight potential growth through media rights and demographic advantages.

MAIN INSIGHTS
• Insight 1: Liga MX is the most viewed soccer league in the U.S., with viewership nearly double that of MLS.
• Insight 2: Despite high viewership, Liga MX clubs have significantly lower valuations compared to MLS clubs.
• Insight 3: The Latino population in the U.S., particularly those of Mexican descent, represents a large growth opportunity for Liga MX.
• Insight 4: Liga MX's current model of selling broadcast rights individually by teams limits its overall league value.
• Insight 5: The new Leagues Cup tournament with MLS could increase exposure and drive up league value through joint media rights sales.

FRAMEWORKS & CONCEPTS
• Revenue multiples — A method used to value sports franchises based on the revenues they generate.
• Control and availability premiums — Factors that can increase the valuation of sports franchises beyond historical revenue multiples.

NOTABLE QUOTES
""I was looking at U.S. viewership trends and Liga MX is the most popular [soccer] league in the U.S. in television viewership and TV ratings by a wide margin." — Sam Porter"
""Commercializing and operationalizing media assets is going to be the key for Liga MX — and by proxy, Necaxa — if it wants to make the best use of its current competitive advantage at home and in the U.S.""

ACTION ITEMS
→ Explore strategic investments in Liga MX clubs to capitalize on their growing U.S. viewership.
→ Consider restructuring Liga MX's media rights model to aggregate and enhance league-wide value.

name: Removing “hope” from the sales process
summary:
This episode of the Predictable Revenue Podcast features Sean Rhodes, a sales expert and former combat correspondent, discussing the importance of removing 'hope' from the sales process. The conversation focuses on creating systematic approaches to sales that increase predictability and success, drawing parallels between military operations and sales strategies.

KEY THEMES
• The Danger of Relying on Hope — Salespeople often rely on hope due to unpredictable variables, leading to inconsistent results.
• Systematizing Sales — Implementing structured systems in sales processes can lead to more predictable and successful outcomes.
• Learning from High-Performing Teams — Insights from military operations can be applied to sales to improve performance and predictability.

MAIN INSIGHTS
• Insight 1: Salespeople often rely on hope due to the unpredictable nature of sales calls and meetings.
• Insight 2: High-performing military teams use systems and debriefs to improve; similar methods can enhance sales outcomes.
• Insight 3: Systematic approaches in sales can alleviate pressure on salespeople, allowing them to innovate and be present.
• Insight 4: Sales leaders should provide tools and systems to help sales teams know who to reach out to and what to say.
• Insight 5: Regularly updating sales systems and processes is crucial to adapt to changing environments and improve effectiveness.

FRAMEWORKS & CONCEPTS
• Bulletproof Selling — A concept of applying military precision and systems to sales processes to improve predictability and success.
• Sales Debriefing — A process of reviewing sales calls to identify what went right, what went wrong, and how to improve.

NOTABLE QUOTES
""Hope is not enough to keep people alive on the battlefield, and it's certainly not enough to keep deals alive in the battlefield of business.""
""If you fail to plan, you're planning to fail.""

ACTION ITEMS
→ Implement a structured CRM system to track sales processes and client interactions.
→ Conduct regular debriefs after sales calls to identify areas for improvement and update systems accordingly.

KEY THEMES
• Marketing Fundamentals — The necessity of understanding basic marketing principles like segmentation and positioning.
• Ad Fraud — How bots affect digital advertising and ways to mitigate this issue.
• AI in Marketing — The role of AI as a tool to enhance, not replace, strategic marketing efforts.

MAIN INSIGHTS
• Insight 1: Two-thirds of marketers failed a survey on basic marketing fundamentals, indicating a gap in foundational knowledge.
• Insight 2: Marketers focusing only on promotion struggle to survive in their roles due to a lack of comprehensive strategy.
• Insight 3: AI cannot replace the strategic foundation of marketing, which requires understanding the market and customer behavior.

name: 28 tactics to improve SEO
summary:
This episode provides a comprehensive guide on improving SEO through 28 actionable tactics. It emphasizes the importance of aligning content with search intent, optimizing on-page elements, and leveraging tools like SEOTesting.com to track and experiment with SEO strategies. These insights are crucial for anyone looking to enhance their website's visibility and ranking on search engines.

KEY THEMES
• Search Intent Alignment — Ensuring content matches the searcher's intent to improve rankings.
• On-page SEO Optimization — Techniques for enhancing page elements like titles, meta descriptions, and internal links.
• Continuous Experimentation — Using tools to track and refine SEO strategies over time.

MAIN INSIGHTS
• Insight 1: Matching content with Google's perceived search intent is crucial for ranking improvements.
• Insight 2: Internal linking helps distribute link equity and improve page relevance.
• Insight 3: Optimizing page titles and meta descriptions can indirectly boost rankings by improving click-through rates.

• Insight 5: Creating topic clusters and using expert quotes can strengthen content authority and trust.

FRAMEWORKS & CONCEPTS
• SEO Testing — A method of using time-based and split tests to track SEO experiment results.
• Topic Clusters — A content strategy involving a pillar page and related subpages to improve SEO.

NOTABLE QUOTES
""Page titles make people click (from Google), H1’s make you stay.""
""A basic principle is to use target keywords in the main heading and long-tail variations of keywords in subheadings.""

ACTION ITEMS
→ Use internal links to boost the ranking of target pages by linking from related content.
→ Experiment with page titles and meta descriptions to improve click-through rates.
→ Add structured data to pages to help search engines understand and display content more effectively.
→ Regularly update content with new information and structured data to maintain relevance.

name: The power of sleep
summary:
In this episode of The Knowledge Project Podcast, sleep scientist Matthew Walker delves into the significance of sleep and its impact on our lives. He discusses how to improve sleep quality, manage insomnia, and the importance of different sleep stages, providing listeners with practical advice and insights into sleep science.

KEY THEMES
• Importance of Sleep — Understanding the critical role sleep plays in overall health and brain function.
• Sleep Stages — Exploration of why different stages of sleep are necessary and their evolutionary significance.
• Improving Sleep Quality — Practical tips and strategies to enhance sleep efficiency and manage insomnia.

MAIN INSIGHTS
• Insight 1: No single stage of sleep is more important than the others; each serves a unique function.
• Insight 2: The evolutionary persistence of all sleep stages suggests their fundamental importance.
• Insight 3: Negative associations with the bed, such as wakefulness, can disrupt sleep patterns.
• Insight 4: Sleep efficiency is a measure of the time spent asleep relative to time in bed.
• Insight 5: Continuous learning and adaptation are crucial, as exemplified by Walker's openness to being wrong.

FRAMEWORKS & CONCEPTS
• Sleep Efficiency — The ratio of time spent asleep to time spent in bed, aiming for 100% efficiency.
• Negative Sleep Associations — The concept that negative experiences related to sleep can affect sleep quality.

NOTABLE QUOTES
"“Why would mother nature lie you so vulnerable and unconscious?”"
"“If I’m ever wrong about something, life in general or science specifically, I don’t want to be wrong any longer than I have to be.”"

ACTION ITEMS
→ Break negative associations with the bed by only using it for sleep.
→ Track your sleep efficiency to identify areas for improvement.

name: The 3 realms of a complete marketing strategy
summary:
This episode discusses the importance of integrating brand marketing, growth marketing, and product marketing to create a comprehensive marketing strategy. It highlights the need for marketing leaders to understand and align these domains to ensure that marketing efforts are effective and sustainable, using examples like FanDuel to illustrate the consequences of misalignment.

KEY THEMES
• Integration of Marketing Domains — Emphasizes the need to integrate brand, growth, and product marketing for a cohesive strategy.
• Adaptation to Market Changes — Discusses the importance of adapting marketing strategies in response to internal and external market changes.
• Long-term Strategy vs. Short-term Gains — Highlights the balance between immediate growth marketing results and the long-term impact of brand and product marketing.

MAIN INSIGHTS
• Insight 1: A successful marketing strategy requires the integration of brand marketing, growth marketing, and product marketing.
• Insight 2: Growth marketing can quickly bring in new customers, but without alignment with brand and product marketing, it may lead to high churn rates.
• Insight 3: Marketing strategies must adapt to changes in the competitive landscape, regulatory environment, and consumer behavior.
• Insight 4: FanDuel's experience shows the risks of focusing too heavily on growth marketing without ensuring the product delivers on brand promises.
• Insight 5: Marketing leaders should continuously monitor internal and external factors to identify when strategic shifts are necessary.

FRAMEWORKS & CONCEPTS
• Three Domains of Marketing — Brand marketing, growth marketing, and product marketing must work together for a successful strategy.
• Growth Loops — Mechanisms like paid marketing and user-generated content that drive customer acquisition and retention.

NOTABLE QUOTES
""Marketing teams can operate in a more integrated fashion by interrogating the impact that changes in one domain will have on others.""
""A clear, effective, and evolving marketing strategy is what differentiates great marketing leaders from great marketing contributors.""

ACTION ITEMS
→ Evaluate your current marketing strategy to ensure alignment across brand, growth, and product marketing domains.
→ Regularly assess internal and external factors to determine if strategic shifts are necessary to maintain competitive advantage.

name: A data driven decision making model for businesses
summary:
This episode explores the importance of data-driven decision-making in the modern business environment, emphasizing the role of advanced analytics and machine learning in gaining competitive advantage. It discusses the balance between algorithmic predictions and human expertise, the necessity of interpretability in models, and the strategic considerations for companies in building internal data science capabilities versus outsourcing.

KEY THEMES
• Data-Driven Decision Making — The increasing reliance on data analytics and machine learning to inform business decisions.
• Human vs. Machine — The balance between algorithmic decision-making and human intuition and oversight.
• Model Interpretability — The need for models to be interpretable to ensure effective communication and application in business contexts.

MAIN INSIGHTS
• Insight 1: Advanced analytics and machine learning are crucial for predicting trends and gaining a competitive edge.
• Insight 2: There is a risk of over-reliance on algorithms, which may not account for unique situational nuances.
• Insight 3: Companies must balance predictive accuracy with model interpretability, especially in managerial applications.
• Insight 4: Building internal data science teams can enhance a company's ability to manage data and support decision-making.
• Insight 5: Outsourcing data management can be a flexible solution for companies with limited resources.

FRAMEWORKS & CONCEPTS
• Predictive Models — Algorithms used to forecast trends and behaviors based on historical data.
• Data Science Teams — Internal groups focused on leveraging data analytics to support business decisions.

NOTABLE QUOTES
"The balance between the predictive ability of statistical and machine learning techniques and the expertise of management is a fundamental requirement today."
"Being fully aware of the weaknesses of an algorithm is the first step towards improving it."

ACTION ITEMS
→ Consider building an internal data science team to enhance decision-making capabilities.
→ Evaluate the interpretability of your predictive models to ensure they can be effectively communicated and applied.

name: The 3 types of vistitors based on intent
summary:
This episode delves into the concept of search intent and its critical role in content marketing and SEO. It categorizes search intent into three types: informational, commercial, and navigational, and explains how understanding these can help marketers align their content to meet user needs, ultimately driving traffic and conversions.

KEY THEMES
• Search Intent — Understanding the different types of search intent and their implications for SEO and content marketing.
• Content Alignment — Aligning content with user intent to improve engagement and conversion rates.
• SEO Strategy — The importance of keyword research and search intent in developing effective SEO strategies.

MAIN INSIGHTS
• Insight 1: Search intent can be categorized into informational, commercial, and navigational, each requiring different content strategies.
• Insight 2: Informational intent queries make up 80% of searches and are crucial for top-of-funnel content strategies.
• Insight 3: Commercial intent queries, though only 10% of searches, are highly valuable for conversions and bottom-of-funnel strategies.
• Insight 4: Navigational queries indicate brand awareness and often result in high click-through rates, serving as a 'second homepage' for brands.
• Insight 5: Understanding and leveraging search intent can significantly enhance content marketing effectiveness and SEO performance.

FRAMEWORKS & CONCEPTS
• Search Intent Framework — A categorization of search queries into informational, commercial, and navigational intents to guide content creation.
• Top of Funnel (TOFU), Middle of Funnel (MOFU), Bottom of Funnel (BOFU) — Stages of the marketing funnel that align with different search intents.

NOTABLE QUOTES
"Every keyphrase indicates intent."
"If you want a lot of leads, you have to help a lot of information seekers."

ACTION ITEMS
→ Conduct keyword research to identify the search intent behind phrases and align your content strategy accordingly.
→ Create content that targets informational queries to build brand awareness and future demand.

name: Being the CMO at OrangeTheoryFitness
summary:
Kevin Keith is the Chief Brand Officer for Orangetheory Fitness, the 12-year-old high-growth brand founded in Boca Raton Florida by Ellen Latham, who's brand purpose is to help people live longer, more vibrant lives. And by all counts it seems to be doing that with its science-based performance-oriented one-hour workouts. OTF has 1 million plus members, 1400 studios in 50 states and 26 countries, and more than $1 billion in system revenue.
Kevin has been OTF's Chief Brand Officer for five years. His career path is rich in agency experiences, as well as time on the client side at Coca-Cola and UPS. This conversation is rife with valuable lessons and goes to show how a brand can inspire a customer to join the organization as a leader by living its purpose and inspiring others to do the same. Keith shares how OTF stays relevant and continues to grow in an industry where brands can easily be considered a fad. Plus, building a unified culture within your organization, identifying your customers as real people vs data points, and much more.

name: Growth Masterclass with Blueboard
summary:
In this week’s episode of The Breakout Growth Podcast Sean Ellis and Ethan Garr chat with Kevin Yip, Blueboard’s Co-Founder and Chief Operating Officer. Blueboard is a platform that allows companies to reward employees with amazing experiences; anything from a skydiving adventure to dinner at a Michelin-rated restaurant is fair game. How does a company with such a unique business concept not only achieve product/market fit but stay dynamic enough to retain it through challenging times? In this episode, we find out.
While entrepreneurs often dream of bringing new ideas to market that nobody else has thought of, it can be a huge challenge to get from zero to one with a completely new idea. Kevin and his co-founder had their work cut out for them in their early days. They literally went door-to-door to try to get companies and their HR teams excited about the value of Blueboard experiences. An intro into GoPro proved to be a boon for the fledgling business, and eventually, Blueboard’s vision of an experience marketplace came to life.
The team continued to dial-in product/market fit. They learned how to more effectively sell into HR, they developed feedback loops to ensure that as employees enjoyed Blueboard rewards they were able to effectively share their experiences with their colleagues and more. The company had found its footing and was on a roll and then Covid hit. But Kevin’s team understood their product/market fit and quickly figured out how they could continue to bring value to employers and their employees in the new stay-at-home environment.

name: Developing strenght through character
summary:
This episode features Dr. Angela Duckworth discussing her research on character development and its impact on personal and social well-being. She elaborates on the three dimensions of character—Heart, Mind, and Will—and emphasizes the importance of cultivating character strengths throughout life. The conversation also touches on the distinction between values and character, and the role of self-awareness in personal growth.

KEY THEMES
• Character Development — Exploring the dimensions of character and their importance in personal and social contexts.
• Grit and Character — Understanding grit as a component of character and its role in achieving excellence.
• Self-awareness and Growth — The significance of self-awareness in identifying and improving character strengths.

MAIN INSIGHTS
• Insight 1: Character is multifaceted, encompassing ways of thinking, acting, feeling, and doing that benefit both oneself and others.
• Insight 2: The three dimensions of character are Heart (interpersonal strengths), Mind (intellectual strengths), and Will (self-regulation and perseverance).
• Insight 3: Grit is an important aspect of character but should be viewed as part of a broader character framework.
• Insight 4: Self-awareness is crucial for identifying and addressing both known and unknown character flaws.
• Insight 5: Small wins and experiences of success are essential for building resilience and confidence.

FRAMEWORKS & CONCEPTS
• Heart, Mind, and Will — Three natural families of character strengths that encompass interpersonal, intellectual, and self-regulatory qualities.
• Psychological Literacy — The concept of increasing understanding of psychological principles to enhance self-awareness and empathy.

NOTABLE QUOTES
"Character is plural… It’s ways of thinking, acting, feeling, and doing that benefit others and yourself, that you can continue to cultivate your whole life."
"A life that is well-lived is a life that is done in service to others as well as yourself."

ACTION ITEMS
→ Cultivate self-awareness by engaging in reflective practices like journaling and meaningful conversations.
→ Focus on achieving small wins to build confidence and resilience.

name: Why Pipeline Velocity is the key business metric
summary: Pipeline Velocity determines how fast the flow moves through your funnel” Pipeline Velocity = (Win rate X Annual Contract Value of closed opps (Avg ARR) X Number of qualified opportunities ) / Sales Cycle Lenght ( Number of days in the period) ”. Win rate = deals closed vs deals lost. Playing with those metrics can drive growth & scalability; it gives more flexibility. Then you break it down by pipeline source and calculate the metric for each one. Q&A session: The win rate, ACV & Sales cycle you calculate using closed dates whereas the qualified opps is a date stamp when it enters opp stage (more than 25%). The buyer controls the velocity. KEY THEMES
• The importance of sleep — Understanding how sleep impacts brain and body function.
• Sleep stages — The evolutionary significance and functional importance of different sleep stages.

MAIN INSIGHTS
• Insight 1: Different stages of sleep serve distinct functions and are all important for overall health.
• Insight 2: Sleep efficiency is a measure of the time spent asleep relative to time spent in bed.

• Sleep efficiency — The ratio of time spent asleep to time spent in bed.

MAIN INSIGHTS
• Insight 1: The new data blending engine includes inner, outer, right, and cross join types, expanding beyond the previously available left join.

• Insight 3: Calculated fields can be created at the chart level, but they remain local to each table and cannot use fields from other tables.
• Insight 4: The new join types provide flexibility in data manipulation, allowing for more complex data relationships and analysis.
• Insight 5: The release is expected to be a game changer, similar to the impact of the parameter feature, offering new opportunities for data preparation and reporting.

FRAMEWORKS & CONCEPTS
• Data Blending — Combining data from multiple sources to create a unified data view.
• Join Types — Methods of combining tables, including inner, outer, left, right, and cross joins.

NOTABLE QUOTES
"In my opinion, it is the most important release since the launching of parameters feature."
"No doubt, this new feature is a game changer, opening a lot of possibilities."

ACTION ITEMS
→ Explore the new join types in Looker Studio to enhance your data blending strategies.
→ Consider the performance and maintenance implications when using the new data blending features for data preparation.

name: The NCT framework for better goal setting
summary:
This episode explores the challenges of effective goal-setting within teams and introduces the NCT (Narrative, Commitments, Tasks) framework as a solution. The discussion highlights the importance of strategic clarity, measurable commitments, and actionable tasks to drive real progress and avoid the pitfalls of traditional goal-setting methods like OKRs.

KEY THEMES
• The complexity of goal-setting — Effective goal-setting requires balancing strategy and execution, which is often challenging for teams.
• The vicious cycle of ineffective goals — Teams often set ambitious goals without actionable commitments, leading to failure and increased pressure.
• The NCT framework — A new approach to goal-setting that emphasizes strategic narratives, measurable commitments, and actionable tasks.

MAIN INSIGHTS
• Insight 1: Many teams focus on moving metrics rather than understanding how to create value, leading to ineffective goal-setting.
• Insight 2: The NCT framework helps teams connect strategy with execution by using narratives to provide context and commitments to measure progress.
• Insight 3: Cross-functional collaboration is crucial for achieving goals, as siloed goals often lead to competition rather than cooperation.
• Insight 4: Teams should set goals based on the stage of product development, using discovery, input, output, and outcome goals appropriately.
• Insight 5: Regular check-ins and adaptability are essential to ensure goals remain relevant and achievable, preventing them from becoming political exercises.

FRAMEWORKS & CONCEPTS
• NCT Framework — A goal-setting framework that uses Narratives, Commitments, and Tasks to align strategy and execution.
• OKRs (Objectives and Key Results) — A traditional goal-setting framework that focuses on setting audacious goals but lacks strategic context.

NOTABLE QUOTES
"Valerie Wagoner: 'We had newly defined metrics tied to strategy, but there wasn’t full fluency or conviction throughout the organization on why that metric mattered.'"
"Brian Balfour: 'We hit our WAU goal, but many of the users ended up being in a segment of the market that wasn't aligned to the company strategy.'"

ACTION ITEMS
→ Adopt the NCT framework to improve goal-setting by ensuring goals are strategically aligned and actionable.
→ Encourage cross-functional goal-setting to foster collaboration and shared ownership of outcomes.

name: Why DAOs Matter for business
summary:
Why Businesses Should Consider DAOs
DAOs are what businesses and organizations will likely look like in the future. This is because a DAO democratizes the direction of the organization itself, allowing members of the organization—no matter the role they play—a vote or a say in what the organization does moving forward.
For example, in a traditional limited liability corporation (LLC), the person who formed the LLC is sitting at the top making all of the decisions, and then staff and employees follow a chain. The further down the chain you go, the less say you have and the less influence you hold over where that organization goes. All or most of the power within the organization lies at the top, which means that the mission of the organization can change at any point.
In a DAO, everybody from the creator to the newest members who purchased into the DAO has a say and vote in any changes made within the organization. You have to agree to the current terms and direction to buy into the organization, which brings like-minded people and investors together to form the DAO, and once in, any changes can only come about through a majority consensus of all the members.
One of the major benefits of a DAO is that it brings like-minded individuals together to fund and support your organization, which ensures that your goals are shared by your investors.
It also removes a lot of intermediary positions, saving you money. As you’re forming the DAO, you don’t have to rely on a lot of third parties to make decisions or ensure that things will go a certain way, including legal costs and other typical startup costs. Essentially, you can build a smart contract to help you automate everything that’s happening based on the decisions being made by the votes as they take place.
Once something is voted on, it automatically goes into effect thanks to these smart contracts. So you don’t need a third-party mediator, which is going to help cut out a lot of costs.

name: Tackling 5 B2B eCommerce Myths
summary:
McKinsey looks at 5 myths around B2B eCommerce and tackles them with data. The best part though, is their recommendations at the end: Lean into B2B e-commerce or be sidelined: With potentially a third of sales at stake, e-commerce is a vital lynchpin for continued B2B revenue growth. If you don’t currently offer an online sales channel, ramp up that capability now.
Win the journey, not just the transaction: Corporate decision makers are turning to e-commerce at every stage of the buying process, from research to reorders, and will walk away if the experience doesn’t deliver what they need.
Don’t settle for easy: Rather than being daunted by learning curves, tackle them methodically, prioritizing critical capabilities and partnering closely with key distributors.
Design your site with million-dollar transactions in mind: Treat e-commerce as a full-service destination and design the online experience to support big- and small-ticket sales.
Recognize that e-commerce is an ecosystem play: Leading B2Bs maximize their online “surface area,” recognizing that the more avenues they can use to get in front of customers, the better. A well-rounded e-commerce presence will include a specific marketplace and partner strategy.

name: Customer Listening: How & Why you need to talk to customers
summary:
